strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and visually appealing problem: adding realistic, dynamic global weather effects (such as snow, rain, fog, and sandstorms) and falling objects into static reconstructed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes.
The proposed hybrid framework successfully combines physics-based simulation (using the Material Point Method via Taichi) with 3DGS primitives, allowing for realistic particle motion and dynamics.

The inclusion of custom, effect-specific collision handling techniques (such as snow accumulation on surfaces, 3D wetness grids for rain darkening, and anisotropic scaling for sand accumulation) significantly enhances visual realism over standard particle systems.
The framework extends well to object-centric dynamics by attaching complex generated 3D models (from text-to-3D generators like GaussianDreamer) to individual simulated particles.
The manuscript is well-structured, clear, and provides extensive implementation and parameter details in the appendix, ensuring excellent reproducibility.
weaknesses: The interactions are strictly one-way. Dynamic weather particles react to the static scene geometry, but the scene itself does not react to the weather (e.g., wind does not blow leaves on trees, rain does not make puddles on the ground). This is a known limitation but restricts the overall realism of the simulation.

The rain wetness effect is modeled by simply darkening the static Gaussians. While this is a reasonable heuristic, actual wet surfaces exhibit complex physical changes like increased specularity and reduced roughness, which are not captured by simple color/opacity adjustments of static Gaussians.

The quantitative evaluation relies on image-level semantic metrics (CLIP similarity, VQAScore) against static editing baselines. While these show the edited frames match the textual prompt, they do not evaluate temporal consistency or the physical plausibility of the simulated motion. A user study or evaluation of motion/trajectory plausibility would make the validation stronger.

Technically, the pipeline is largely a combination of existing techniques: mesh extraction from 2DGS, MPM simulation from PhysGaussian/Feature Splatting, and model generation from GaussianDreamer. The main novelty lies in the integration and the specific heuristic post-processing rules for collision handling.

strengths: The paper introduces an innovative and practical framework that integrates physics-based Material Point Method (MPM) simulations with 3D Gaussian Splatting to animate static scenes with dynamic, interactive weather effects.

The specialized collision handling techniques are well-designed and effective: the 3D wetness grid for rainfall and the surface projection for snow/sand accumulation greatly enhance the visual realism of the physical interactions.

The approach is versatile and extends beyond global weather phenomena to object-level physics (such as falling leaves or landing drones) by utilizing 3D generative priors (GaussianDreamer) controlled by a single simulated particle.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations of the three-stage pipeline and comprehensive implementation details provided in the appendix, ensuring reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as it heavily combines existing building blocks: 3DGS, mesh extraction from 2DGS, and MPM simulation via the Taichi framework.

The quantitative evaluation is restricted to static-image editing metrics (CLIP similarity, VQAScore). While these capture appearance alignment, they are insufficient for evaluating temporal consistency, video quality, or physical realism.

The simulation and collision handling depend heavily on the quality of the extracted mesh from the static 3DGS. For complex or noisy outdoor environments, incomplete or inaccurate geometry reconstruction could significantly degrade the accuracy of the physical collisions and accumulation effects.
The current rendering and simulation speed (7 FPS on an RTX A5000) does not achieve real-time rates, which partially compromises one of the primary benefits of using 3DGS.

strengths: The application of adding dynamic, interactive weather effects (such as snow, rain, and sandstorms) to static 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes is highly practical and visually appealing for virtual production, gaming, and VR.

The hybrid representation—simulating dynamics using a particle-based Material Point Method (MPM) and converting them back to Gaussian primitives for rendering—successfully leverages the physical plausibility of particle simulations and the high-fidelity rendering of 3DGS.

The effect-specific collision handling techniques (such as the 3D wetness grid for rain and normal-based projection for snow accumulation) show creative engineering to handle the coarseness of grid-based MPM simulations.
weaknesses: Limited Technical Novelty: The core pipeline is largely a combination of existing tools and methods. It utilizes standard 3DGS [18] for reconstruction, TSDF fusion [12] for mesh extraction, Taichi MPM [11] (similar to PhysGaussian [41] and Feature Splatting [30]) for physical simulation, and GaussianDreamer [43] for object asset generation. The novelty of the integration itself is incremental.

Heavy Reliance on Manual Tuning and Heuristics: Achieving the final visual quality requires extensive manual intervention. The appearance parameters (color, scale, opacity, elongation) are manually set on a per-scene and per-effect basis. The collision handling also relies on handcrafted heuristics (e.g., manually shifting particles along normals, applying manual exponential decay to the wetness grid) rather than unified physical principles.

Unfair/Inappropriate Baseline Comparisons: The quantitative and qualitative evaluations heavily compare against static 3D editing methods (ClimateNeRF [21] and GaussCtrl [38]). Because these baselines are static appearance editors, comparing them on dynamic animation tasks naturally makes the proposed dynamic approach look superior. A more appropriate baseline would be simulating particles (like snow or rain) using traditional graphics engines (e.g., Blender, Unity, or Unreal Niagara) on the extracted mesh of the 3DGS scene and rendering them alongside the static Gaussians.

Evaluation Metrics Do Not Measure Dynamics: The quantitative evaluation in Table 1 relies on 2D semantic metrics (CLIP similarity, CLIP direction similarity, and VQAScore) calculated on static frames. These metrics do not evaluate the physical correctness, temporal consistency, or the realism of the simulated motion.

Performance Bottleneck: The runtime of the proposed pipeline is 7 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX A5000. This is a significant bottleneck compared to the real-time (100+ FPS) rendering advantage of typical 3DGS pipelines, limiting its applicability for interactive or real-time applications.
